extracted.intended_audience: junior college journalism instructors and students (newswriting/reporting courses)
extracted.subtask_description: Instructional objectives and evaluation criteria for two junior college courses: Journalism 20A (Newswriting & Reporting) and 20B (Advanced Newswriting). Covers learning goals, measurable objectives, grading policy, story/evaluation checklists, production and beat-specific rubrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course grading policy (J20A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentage breakdown for course grade: Participation/on class issue of Branding Iron 20%; Unit tests and midterm 20%; Class assignments 30%; Final exam 10%; News quizzes 5%; Class participation 10%; Press conferences 5%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To receive an A/B/C students must meet stated standards. Stories must be corrected and returned or they receive assigned zeros; late work may be dropped one grade unless approved. Grading examples illustrate how weighted components combine to an average.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course grading policy (J20B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Percentage breakdown for Advanced Newswriting: Stories you cover 40%; Scrapbook (clippings) 15%; Class assignments 20%; Participation 15%; News quizzes 5%; Mid-term/final 5%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewrites allowed on stories you cover (average of two grades or higher of two); late stories are dropped one grade. To receive an 'A' criteria spelled out (e.g., stories all on time with average grade high B, scrapbook all 13 in, class participation regular/informed, midterm/final 80% correct).

rubrics_metrics.name: Late submission penalty
rubrics_metrics.description: All late stories will be dropped one grade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless previously approved by instructor; lateness policies appear repeatedly across course sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewrites policy
rubrics_metrics.description: On stories you cover, stories may be rewritten to improve grade; you will receive the average of two grades or you may cover another event and receive the higher of the two grades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy applies to J20B; gives students option to rewrite or re-cover to improve grade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic failure for misspelling a name
rubrics_metrics.description: Misspelling a name gives an automatic 'F' on a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit hard rule repeated in course materials; emphasizes extreme importance of accurate identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: News story content checklist (selection & structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the 'most important' item skillfully and present it early; ensure facts are correct and clear; write to catch the reader's interest; follow through smoothly from lead to body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used in NEWS STORY CHECK SHEET and units: the 'most important' item should be selected and presented; leads should catch reader and the body should follow logically (inverted pyramid or appropriate structure).

rubrics_metrics.name: News story fairness and objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories must be fair and objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fairness/objectivity evaluated as part of content checklist and beat-specific evaluation; students practice analyzing ethical issues via class discussion and clipping exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy (facts and identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Facts must be correct and clear; identification (especially in accidents, disasters, death/illness) must be accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy is repeatedly emphasized as a primary criterion for grading stories; errors in identification carry heavy penalties (e.g., misspelled names = F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest / newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Write to catch readers' interest; assess stories for interest and newsworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied across beats and assignments (clip-and-evaluate, story grading). Students expected to choose leads and angles that maximize relevance and interest, including 'Keep it Local', 'Keep it Current', 'Make it Count'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead quality (selection and writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leads must select the most important item, be interesting and informative, and lead into a logically ordered body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises include rewriting poor leads, writing feature leads, and scoring leads on accuracy and attractiveness; unit tests and lab exercises measure improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow-through / transitions / organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Body copy must follow through smoothly from lead, use clear transitions, and exhibit good organization and design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NEWS STORY CHECK SHEET items include 'Follows through smoothly' and 'Transitions'; students practice through assignments and unit tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style: economical word use and word choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Economical word use; careful choice of words to present stories both accurately and interestingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students complete worksheets and assignments to improve word usage; examples given (cross out unnecessary words, improve poor ones). Word usage tested with target accuracies (e.g., 70% on test questions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar and mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct grammar, spelling, and punctuation are required in all work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectives specify correcting at least 80% of grammatical errors on unit tests, use of Strunk & White and AP Stylebook encouraged; misspellings penalized harshly.

rubrics_metrics.name: AP Style and copyediting (punctuation, capitalization, abbreviations, numerals, titles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize and apply rules of punctuation, capitalization, abbreviations, use of numerals, correct spellings, and use of titles as outlined in the AP Stylebook.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lab and unit test objectives: correct at least 70% on worksheets (may use Stylebook & dictionary), 80% on unit tests. Use of Stylebook and dictionary permitted for exercises and tests where noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copyreading symbols proficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Student will use basic copyreading symbols to correct errors and give directions to printer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required accuracy on copyreading symbols: 60% on unit test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline writing (heads)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write applicable, concise headlines; each acceptable head must have a subject and verb; head length limits will be stated and must be observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Head-count limits specified per assignment and must be observed 100%; exercises include writing suggested heads for stories and heads on unit tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page makeup / dummy page layout
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand basic rules for page makeup: draw page 1 dummy showing story positions, head sizes and slugs, art with slugs and captions, and relation to masthead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments require producing dummy pages copied from recent Branding Iron issues and proposing page 1 layouts; peer critique included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production / editor's responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors have final responsibility for accuracy; they must ensure copy is marked correctly for the printer, write heads, dummy pages, and assign stories and editing tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students assigned editorial roles must manage assignments, editing, head/caption writing, makeup, editorial conferences, and production in shop. Non-editing students must meet deadlines and style/accuracy rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication responsibilities and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Students will produce an issue of the Branding Iron: editors assume executive roles and all students complete minimum assignments for the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment based on meeting editor/production responsibilities, deadlines, style rules, accuracy, and the editor's decisions on length and need for rewriting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics and libel knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Students will know and be able to apply basic concepts and laws of libel and journalistic ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unit tests require 70% correct on multiple-choice statements concerning libel; exercises include identifying apparently libelous or unethical statements and explaining editorial decisions in short written responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsroom organization and lines of responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the typical newsroom set-up and line of authority and apply it to student newspaper production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class discussions and unit tests on newspaper organization (expected to complete 70% of multiple-choice statements); exercises include selecting editors and assigning duties in class-run Branding Iron editions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clip-and-evaluate rubric (common to beats)
rubrics_metrics.description: When clipping and evaluating published stories students should assess presentation, accuracy, completeness, interest (and where applicable fairness and level of government).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clip-and-evaluate method is applied across beats (editorials, speeches, police, courts, politics, government, women's pages, sports, entertainment, business, science) with occasional beat-specific additions (e.g., number of quotes/paraphrases for speech stories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat-specific evaluation criteria (general pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beat stories are evaluated on interest, accuracy, completeness, and presentation; some beats add criteria such as fairness (courts), number of quotes/paraphrases (speeches), or clarity in explaining technical information (science).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each beat assignment lists which of these common criteria will be used to grade student work; students are to list sources for police stories and demonstrate knowledge of court/judicial reporting responsibilities when covering courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial writing rubric
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials must be opinion pieces based on fact: include factual basis for the editorial, state main point of view, present major supporting arguments and a conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments: clip an editorial and note facts used, main point, major arguments, and write a brief critique; then research and write an original editorial (1–1.5 pages) evaluated on inclusion of opinion, factual basis, support, and conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview reporting rubric
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews should be evaluated/graded for general presentation, use of interview material, completeness and accuracy; students must demonstrate ability to participate in news conferences and produce stories based on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Objectives include clipping interview stories for analysis, participating in class news conferences, asking pertinent questions, and producing publishable copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speech reporting rubric
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories based on speeches are graded for interest, accuracy, number of quotes and paraphrases, descriptive detail (speaker, crowd), and overall importance of the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students clip and analyze speech-based stories and are assigned to cover speeches with emphasis on applying these criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accidents/disasters and death/illness reporting criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories in these categories demand extreme accuracy in identification and are graded on presentation, accuracy, completeness and interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students clip relevant stories for critique and write pieces from fact sheets graded on completeness and accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Police reporting criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Police beat work should be evaluated for presentation, accuracy, completeness and interest; students may be required to list sources (police blotter, desk sergeant, detective, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments include feature projects (e.g., ride-alongs) or writing from police fact sheets; work graded on specified factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court reporting criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Court coverage assessed for accuracy, fairness, completeness and interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students clip court trial stories for analysis and write stories from trials or sessions they attend; emphasis on judicial system knowledge and appropriate reporting etiquette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science reporting criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Science stories must be accurate, complete, interesting, and present scientific information in common terms so readers can understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students clip interpretative science reports for critique and write science stories from fact sheets or press conferences with grading on accuracy, clarity, and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sports reporting criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Sports reports are graded on interest, accuracy, completeness and any special writing style required for sports writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students expected to attend events and submit reports evaluated by these criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business and labor reporting criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Business and labor stories graded on accuracy, newsworthiness, interest and completeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work may originate from press conferences or releases; students must demonstrate ability to handle specialized information and assess newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting angles, localizing and timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters should select appropriate angles (especially local angles) and handle running/breaking stories by asking what is new, accurate, and of interest now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments include selecting lead angles for given fact sets and writing leads that emphasize timely/local relevance; evaluated in unit tests and press conference exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretative reporting skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the term 'interpretative reporting' and apply techniques to make facts meaningful for readers (depth, context, analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments include finding examples, writing critiques and applying interpretative techniques in assigned stories; MacDougall chapters assigned as reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment format and length requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Many written assignments must be typed, double-spaced with specified length ranges (e.g., news stories 1–2 pages, feature stories 1–3 pages, editorials 1–1.5 pages).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting requirements are enforced; failure to meet format/length expectations can affect grading and adherence to editor directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery thresholds on tests and exercises
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific accuracy thresholds are used as objective measures: e.g., unit tests—grammar correction 80%; unit test style corrections 80%; lab worksheet style corrections 70%; libel multiple-choice 70%; weekly news quizzes often require ~60% correct on specified items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These numeric targets are part of the course's behavioral objectives to translate learning outcomes into measurable terms; use of Stylebook/dictionary allowed where specified.
